messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Delivery Driver
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 48

**Case Vignette: Mr. D.**

Mr. D. is a 77-year-old married man who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his wife, Eleanor. He is a retired delivery driver for a regional furniture company, a job he held for over forty years. He describes himself as a man who “never had a problem with anyone” and who took pride in his punctuality and friendly demeanor on his route. He is softly spoken, with a slight tremor in his hands that he attributes to “nerves,” and he maintains rigid, upright posture throughout the session, as if bracing for impact.

The event that changed everything occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Mr. D. was making a final delivery to a suburban home in the early evening. As he was carrying a heavy armoire up the front steps, a man—later identified as a neighbor in the throes of a psychotic episode—ran at him from the side of the house, screaming incoherently. The man struck Mr. D. twice in the head and face with a metal pipe. Mr. D. fell backward, the armoire crushing his leg. He remembers lying on the concrete, unable to move, watching the man stand over him and raise the pipe again. A bystander intervened, and the assailant fled. Mr. D. sustained a fractured orbital bone, a concussion, and a broken tibia. He spent three weeks in the hospital.

In the months since, Mr. D. has not returned to work. He retired early, a decision that felt like a defeat. He tells me he cannot even walk past the loading dock at the old depot without his heart “slamming into his throat.” He now lives in a state of constant, low-grade vigilance. He has stopped taking his daily walk to the corner store, a ritual he enjoyed for decades. “I see every shadow as a man with a pipe,” he says, his voice flat. “I see the shape of his shoulders. I hear his shoes on the pavement before I see him.”

At home, Mr. D. is withdrawn. He sits in a recliner facing the front door, a position from which he can monitor all windows. He has asked Eleanor to lock the screen door, a door that was never locked in forty-seven years of marriage. He sleeps poorly, waking several times a night from a recurring dream in which he is pinned to the ground, unable to scream. He experiences intrusive images during the day—the glint of the pipe, the pattern of the concrete against his cheek—that cause him to freeze mid-sentence or drop whatever he is holding. He has become irritable, snapping at Eleanor for trivial things, like the sound of her chewing or the volume of the television. He feels guilty about this, but says he feels “a switch flip” inside him that he cannot control.

He avoids all reminders of the event. He will not drive past the house where it happened, even if it adds twenty minutes to a trip. He has stopped watching the evening news, because stories of violence send him into a cold sweat. He feels emotionally numb, describing a sense of being “behind glass” while the rest of the world moves on. He no longer feels pleasure in his woodworking hobby, and he has stopped attending his weekly poker game with old friends. “They don’t want to hear about it,” he says. “And I don’t want to talk about it. So I just stay home.”

He reports feeling “old for the first time in my life.” He is hypervigilant of his own body, checking for pain in his leg and head, interpreting every ache as a sign that the damage is permanent. He feels a pervasive sense of a foreshortened future, telling me, “I don’t plan anything anymore. What’s the point? You can’t see it coming.”

Eleanor reports that he has become “a ghost in the house.” She is worried he is depressed, but Mr. D. insists he is not sad. “I’m scared,” he corrects her, and then he looks at the floor. “I’m scared all the time. And I’m tired of being scared.”
